title: Decision trees
blurb: An AI you can actually read — grow a tree of yes/no questions and watch it sort a pile of pets.

steps.title: The AI you can read
steps.body:
Some AIs are a mystery box — they give an answer but can't explain *why*.

A **decision tree** is the opposite. It sorts things with a chain of simple **yes/no questions**, like a game of 20 Questions. Each question is a **split** that cuts a pile into two. You're about to grow one yourself.

steps.title: Grow your tree
steps.body: Here's a pile of pets — cats, dogs and rabbits — with their weight, ear length and tail length. **Click a leaf**, pick a measurement and a cut, and **Add split**. Keep splitting the messy leaves until your tree sorts almost all of them. Watch the accuracy climb!

steps.title: Look what you did
steps.body:
Notice how **one split was never enough** — you had to keep asking another question on each side, and the tree got deeper and smarter. That branching shape is exactly why it's called a *tree*.

And each split you added split the pile a little **cleaner** — that's the whole game: a tree always hunts for the question that separates the groups best.

steps.title: Its superpower: you can explain it
steps.body:
Here's what makes trees special. If your tree says *"this is a rabbit,"* it can show exactly **why**: *"because its tail was short, and it was light."* You can read the path.

That's called being **explainable** (a "white box"). Doctors, banks and judges love trees for this — when an AI affects someone's life, being able to explain the *why* really matters.

steps.title: Why trees?
steps.question: Why might a hospital prefer a decision tree over a mystery-box AI?
choices: You can see and explain exactly why it made each decision
steps.explain: Explainability! A tree shows its reasoning step by step — crucial when a decision affects a real person.

steps.title: What you built 🎉
steps.body:
You grew a real decision tree:

- It sorts things with a chain of **yes/no questions** (splits)
- **More branches = smarter** — one split is rarely enough
- Each split aims to separate the groups **cleanest**
- Its superpower is being **explainable** — it can always show its reasoning

Want to go deeper? The **Decision Tree Studio** has the same build with a held-out test set, so you can watch *overfitting* happen. **Next up:** neural networks — teach a tiny digital 'brain' to learn.
